sources.entry: Reconciling High Server Utilization and Sub-millisecond Quality-of-Service - Shows the tail, not throughput, caps a latency-critical server's utilisation, and how far co-located work lowers it.

summary.title: Reconciling High Server Utilization and Sub-millisecond Quality-of-Service
summary.one_liner: Co-locating batch work with a latency-critical memcached server can raise utilization without breaking sub-millisecond QoS, if queuing, scheduling and load-imbalance interference are addressed.
keywords: how to run batch jobs on latency-sensitive servers
takeaways: Low tail latency, not raw throughput, is what limits how far a latency-critical server can be utilised.
Co-location causes QoS violations through three channels: queuing delay from shared-resource interference, scheduling delay from timesharing cores, and thread load imbalance.
Interference-aware provisioning turns interference into a predictable throughput reduction rather than latency spikes.
A modern BVT scheduler gives more predictable latency and fair CPU sharing than Linux CFS in the paper's co-location tests.
Thread pinning and NIC flow-affinity interrupt routing reduce memcached's sensitivity to load imbalance; the paper reports up to 52% higher throughput per TCO dollar from co-location.
summary.summary: The paper studies whether latency-critical services with sub-millisecond QoS can share servers with other workloads without losing good tail latency. It uses memcached as a representative service, measuring its request pipeline on a dual-socket Xeon server under Linux 3.5 with the mutilate load generator. It breaks co-location interference into queuing delay, scheduling delay and thread load imbalance, and proposes mitigations such as interference-aware provisioning, a BVT-style scheduler, and thread pinning with IRQ affinity. The authors estimate co-location could improve datacenter throughput per TCO dollar by up to 52%.
